# Diagnosing Intermittent Power Loss in a 1999 Jeep Grand Cherokee

A sudden drop in RPMs followed by a brief power surge is a classic symptom of an interruption in the engine's air-fuel mixture or ignition timing. Since you've already addressed the fuel and air filters, we can rule out gross clogging issues. The fact that there is no check engine light is significant; it suggests the Engine Control Module (ECM) either isn't detecting a fault severe enough to trigger a lamp, or the fault is intermittent enough that it hasn't set a permanent code yet. In modern systems like those in a 1999 Grand Cherokee with the 4.0L inline-six or 5.2L V8, this behavior often points toward a failing fuel pressure regulator, a clogged return line, or an issue within the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor circuit.

When the engine loses power for exactly five seconds and then recovers, it strongly indicates a momentary loss of fuel delivery. The ECM attempts to compensate by opening the throttle wider or enriching the mixture, which explains the "short burst" you feel afterward before the system crashes again. If this were an ignition misfire due to worn spark plugs or coils, you would likely hear rough idling or see a specific P030x code stored in memory. However, since the engine feels sluggish constantly while only seizing up under load, the root cause is likely related to fuel pressure stability rather than static delivery.

One common failure point on these vehicles is the electric fuel pump inside the tank losing performance as it heats up or ages. The pump may struggle to maintain the required 35–40 psi during high-demand acceleration events. If the fuel filter was recently replaced, ensure that the replacement unit has an adequate bypass valve; some aftermarket filters can restrict flow too much if they are not rated for high-volume applications, though this is less likely given your mileage and filter history.

Another possibility involves the vacuum modulator on the intake manifold or a stuck throttle body position sensor (TPS). On older GM-based ECUs like the Jeep 24-pin system, a faulty TPS can send erratic voltage spikes to the ECM, causing it to momentarily cut fuel injection as a safety precaution. You can verify this by checking the electrical connector at the throttle body for signs of corrosion or loose pins. A multimeter reading across the TPS wires while someone slowly opens the throttle should show a smooth, linear increase in millivolts. Any jagged jumps correlate directly with the RPM drop you are experiencing.

Additionally, check the condition of the fuel pressure regulator return line. If this hose is cracked internally or has a pinhole leak, fuel will dump back into the tank rather than returning to the manifold when pressure spikes during acceleration. This creates a cyclical effect where pressure builds, leaks out, drops below threshold, causes the power loss, and then the pump builds pressure again until it leaks once more. Inspect this line for wet spots or softness that indicates internal degradation.

If these mechanical checks yield nothing, consider scanning the data stream from an OBDII interface while reproducing the issue. Look specifically at the Short Term Fuel Trim (STFT) values. If you see the STFT hitting +25% or higher during the power loss event, it confirms the ECM is trying to compensate for a lean condition caused by insufficient fuel pressure or airflow mismeasurement. Without live data access, diagnosis relies on listening for fuel pump whine changes and feeling throttle response lag before the engine dies momentarily.
